newsitem.title: FRANCE: Ex-Mitterrand aide sees judge in bugging probe.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Mitterrand aide sees judge in bugging probe.

text.p: A senior aide to late French president Francois Mitterrand told a judge on Friday he was prepared to breach official secrecy to answer questions about alleged illegal wiretapping under the former Socialist leader.

Gilles Menage, former head of Mitterrand's private office, said after four hours of questioning by investigating magistrate Jean-Paul Valat: "I confirmed to the judge my decision to set aside the duty of official secrecy to answer his questions."

Menage is under investigation for allegedly authorising an anti-terrorism unit in Mitterrand's office to carry out widespread illegal wiretapping of journalists, lawyers and politicians from 1982 to 1986.
He told reporters he had named a first list of 10 to 15 people on whom he was prepared to explain the grounds for wiretapping, out of 150 for which he is being investigated.
Among them he cited investigative journalist Edwy Plenel of the newspaper Le Monde, lawyer Antoine Comte and writer Jean-Edern Hallier, who died recently.
Plenel said Menage's disclosures was tantamount to admitting, after years of denials, that "journalists and lawyers were bugged, not as terrorists, but because they were doing their work".
"This was a practice worthy of totalitarian regimes, not of democracy," he said, calling on legislators to curb presidential powers.
Menage said he would not disclose information that could endanger state security or personnel.

In an apparent attempt to shield France's present conservative rulers, he said he would not reveal secrets involving the 1986-1988 "cohabitation" period when conservative President Jacques Chirac was Mitterrand's prime minister.
Prime Minister Alain Juppe reacted angrily on Thursday to Menage's decision to breach state secrecy, punishable by up to seven years in jail and a 700,000 franc ($120,000) fine.

"Taking account of the legitimate concerns expressed by the prime minister I told (the judge) that if our exchanges touched on state security or the security of people, naturally I would respect that absolute obligation," Menage said.
Menage said he would not reveal the names of people who work for the government communications interception centre (GIC) which conducted the wiretaps.
But the judge was not prepared to accept a blanket refusal to answer questions invoking state secrecy, he said.
Menage said media reports had grossly exaggerated the number of people whose telephones were bugged. The anti-terrorist unit had wiretapped some 80 people annually.
In a series of media interviews, Menage said the prime ministers and defence ministers between 1983 and 1986 had authorised the contested wiretapping and were politically responsible for it.
French media have reported that up to 2,000 were victims of wiretapping by the Elysee palace unit. The daily Liberation said some 100,000 people were being illegally wiretapped each year.
Mitterrand, who served from 1981 to 1995, died last year of prostate cancer just eight months after leaving office.
